planting.note: Plant container-grown or balled-and-burlapped specimens in spring or fall into humus-rich, well-drained soil in full sun to light shade; this graceful small tree struggles in hot, dry, or alkaline sites.

directions: Plant in cool, humus-rich, well-drained soil in full sun to light shade; this western Chinese species forms a small, airy tree with finely divided, fern-like pinnate leaves that color well in autumn. Dangling clusters of small berries open rosy-pink and fade through the season to blush-white, a softer, longer-lasting display than the typical scarlet rowan. Best suited to cool-summer climates and resents compacted or poorly drained ground.

planting.note: Plant container-grown specimens in spring or fall into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; site where the winter berry display can be viewed from indoors.

directions: Grow in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; native to the Himalaya and Kashmir, this small tree opens pale pink flower clusters in late spring followed by marble-sized, pure white berries that hang on bare branches well into winter, a striking departure from the red or orange fruit of most rowans. Fern-like leaflets turn soft yellow-orange before fall. The persistent white fruit is a late-season draw for waxwings and other winter birds once other food sources are depleted.

planting.note: Plant grafted or container-grown specimens in spring or fall into well-drained soil in full sun; the upright, narrow habit suits small gardens and street-tree plantings where space is limited.

directions: Plant in well-drained soil in full sun; this long-cultivated selection, named for the plant collector who first distributed it, produces an upright, narrowly oval tree with pinnate foliage. Dense clusters of amber-yellow berries ripen in late summer and often persist after the leaves have turned a striking mix of orange, red, and purple in autumn. Its tidy, columnar habit makes it one of the most widely planted ornamental rowans in temperate gardens.

planting.note: Plant container-grown clumps in spring into acidic to neutral, well-drained soil; the plant spreads slowly by underground suckers to form a low colony.

directions: Plant in acidic to neutral, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; native to mountain thickets of Yunnan and northern Myanmar, this low suckering shrub is a true miniature rowan, spreading gradually into dense patches rather than growing as a tree. Small clusters of berries open dark red and fade to pink-blushed white by autumn, set against foliage that turns bronze-purple before falling. Useful as a textured groundcover or low border shrub in cool-climate gardens.

planting.note: Propagate only from stem cuttings taken after flowering, since the fully double blooms are sterile and set no viable seed; plant rooted cuttings into lean, alkaline, sharply drained soil in full sun.

directions: Grow in lean, sharply drained, neutral to alkaline soil in full sun; this old double-flowered wallflower has been propagated continuously by cuttings since at least the Victorian era, since its congested, fully double mustard-yellow flowers never set seed. Dense rounded spikes of bloom open in mid-spring with a light clove-like fragrance, held above gray-green lance-shaped leaves. Plants are short-lived and prone to decline after a few years, so rooting fresh cuttings periodically keeps the clone in circulation; excellent for dry walls, raised beds, and cottage-garden borders.

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring into consistently moist, humus-rich soil; this species blooms later in the season than most garden burnets.

directions: Plant in consistently moist, humus-rich soil in partial sun; native to wet meadows and streambanks of Japan, this naturally white-flowered burnet (distinct from white-flowered color forms of other Sanguisorba species) sends up slender, wiry stems topped with dense, nodding bottlebrush spikes in late summer. Finely divided, blue-green compound leaves form a tidy clump below the bloom stalks. Pairs well with other moisture-loving perennials in a rain garden or pondside border, and the flower spikes are attractive to late-season pollinators.

planting.note: Root stem-tip cuttings or plant container-grown specimens in well-drained, average soil in full sun to partial shade a few weeks before last frost; thrives in cool weather and may stall in peak summer heat.

directions: Plant in well-drained, average soil in full sun to partial shade; this South African species has a more vigorous, trailing habit than the common hybrid twinspurs, sending out long stems that root readily where they touch soil. Dense whorled spikes of deep rose-pink, twin-spurred flowers cluster toward the stem tips through cool spring and fall weather. Excellent for spilling over wall tops, raised beds, or large containers; cut back hard after the first flush to encourage a second round of bloom.
